newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac convenes top ministers over Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chirac convenes top ministers over Zaire crisis.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac consulted senior officials on the crisis in Zaire on Wednesday, as Paris disclosed that an envoy held secret talks with ailing Zairean leader Mobutu Sese Seko in Switzerland last week.
Chirac convened top cabinet ministers for an unscheduled meeting, presidential aides said.

Earlier a Spanish Foreign Ministry spokesman revealed Madrid and Paris were planning to send a multinational force of at least 5,000 troops to the region to help get emergency aid to a million starving refugees in Zaire.

The French Foreign Ministry revealed that Chirac had sent his chief aide Dominique de Villepin to Lausanne last Thursday to meet Mobutu, who had been in Switzerland since August for prostate cancer treatment.

The ministry did not say what the two men discussed, but shortly afterwards France proposed dispatching an international force to help get food and water to refugees displaced by fighting between Zairean troops and Rwanda-backed Tutsi rebels.

Mobutu, once unwelcome in France for delaying a transition to democratic rule in Zaire, left Switzerland for France on Monday and is in seclusion in his Riviera villa, where aides say he planned to convalesce for a few days before returning home.
Mobutu has not made a public statement since fighting broke out in his country.
United Nations envoy Raymond Chretien was to have talks with Mobutu later on Wednesday at the Zairean leader's luxury villa at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin near Nice.

The Spanish foreign ministry spokesman, who asked not to be identified, said that under the Franco-Spanish plan, which would require U.N. approval, France would send about 1,000 troops to northeastern Zaire while Spain would send fewer than 1,000.
The two countries hoped the United States and other nations would contribute thousands more although none has yet committed itself to do so, the spokesman said.

A minimum of 5,000 soldiers would be needed for the operation to save refugees deprived of food by the fighting in the region, the spokesman added. The multinational force would be gradually replaced by African troops under the plan.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt had said earlier on Wednesday that it was premature to discuss how many troops France might contribute to a multinational force.
But he stressed that France's sole goal in participating such an initiative would be to help starving refugees and not to interfere in any way into politics.

France is still smarting from charges from African countries and some of its own European allies its 1994 intervention in neighbouring Rwanda, which it said was intended to help stem genocide, was mainly to advance French policy objectives.
